# v3.30.0

Covers everything since **v3.29**.

The theme is **how this system is versioned and updated**. Nothing about the application itself changes — no new pages, no changed reports, no data touched. What changes is the version number you see, and the choice of how a system receives updates.

You may notice the version number looks different. It now has three parts.

## Changed — version numbers that mean something

Versions are now **MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH** (this one is `3.30.0`):

- the **patch** number moves for fixes,
- the **minor** number for new features,
- the **major** number for a change that alters existing behaviour.

The old scheme was a single counter that advanced by 0.01 every time anything at all was changed, so `3.29` told you nothing about what was in it or whether it mattered to you. A version now carries that information before you read a word of the notes.

A consequence worth knowing: releases will be **less frequent and larger**. Previously every individual fix was published as its own release. Several related changes now arrive together, described in one set of notes written to be read, rather than a stream of entries each covering a single change.

## New — a beta update channel

There are now three channels, set by `UPDATE_CHANNEL` in your `.env` file, and switchable from **Admin → Updates** by clicking the channel badge next to the version number:

| Channel | What it tracks |
|---|---|
| **stable** *(default)* | Published releases. Recommended for live systems. |
| **beta** | Test builds, which appear only when one is deliberately prepared. |
| **dev** | Every change as it is made. Development systems only. |

**beta** is the new one, and it fills a real gap. Previously a non-production system either followed every single change or waited for a full release, with nothing in between. A beta system updates only when a test build is put out — so you can take a build, check it against your own data, and know it will sit still while you do.

Switching channels now also refuses a switch that would move a system **backwards** onto older code, which the previous check could miss.

## Changed — dev and beta systems report what actually changed

A system on **dev** or **beta** no longer waits for a version number to move. **Admin → Updates** tells it how many changes are waiting and lists them, so you can see what an update contains before applying it.

Two things follow from this, both expected rather than faults:

- **A dev or beta system's version number stays put between releases.** The number is the last published release; the list of waiting changes is the live signal.
- **Live systems are unaffected.** A system on **stable** behaves exactly as before — it tracks published releases and updates when one appears.

## For administrators

Nothing to do. Existing systems keep their current channel and update as they always have.

To try the beta channel on a non-production system, set `UPDATE_CHANNEL="beta"` in its `.env`, or switch it from **Admin → Updates**.
